part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Overview & phased commencement (the Act)
body:
Enacted by Parliament; received President's assent **11 August 2023**. Long title: "An Act to provide for the processing of digital personal data in a manner that recognises both the right of individuals to protect their personal data and the need to process such personal data for lawful purposes and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto."

The Act has **9 Chapters, 44 sections, and one Schedule** (penalty table). Source for all section text below: official MeitY PDF (row 1 of source table).

**Commencement status (critical for the chatbot to state correctly):** The Act itself was *not* brought into force on enactment. Section 1(2) empowers the Central Government to notify different commencement dates for different provisions. Via a commencement notification (G.S.R. 843(E), dated 13 November 2025 — see Key Uncertainties for sourcing confidence), the Central Government has brought the Act into force in three phases:
- **Phase 1 (13/14 November 2025, i.e., date of gazette publication):** Section 1(2), Section 2 (definitions), Sections 18–26 (Data Protection Board — establishment, composition, procedure), Sections 35, 38–43 (miscellaneous/general provisions), and Section 44(1) and (3) (consequential amendments to TRAI Act and RTI Act).
- **Phase 2 (one year after publication, i.e., ~13/14 November 2026):** Section 6(9) (mandatory registration of Consent Managers) and Section 27(1)(d) (Board's power to inquire into Consent Manager registration breaches).
- **Phase 3 (eighteen months after publication, i.e., ~13/14 May 2027):** Sections 3–5, Section 6(1)–(8) and (10), Sections 7–17 (the substantive Data Fiduciary obligations and Data Principal rights chapters), Section 27 (except clause (d)), Sections 28–34, 36, 37, and Section 44(2) (IT Act amendments, including omission of Section 43A).

**Practical implication for a compliance chatbot:** As of the compilation date, the *institutional* machinery (Board, penalties architecture, rule-making power) is legally live, but the *core operative obligations* on Data Fiduciaries (notice, consent, children's data safeguards, breach notification duty under s.8(6), Data Principal rights of access/correction/erasure, SDF obligations) do not become legally enforceable until 14 May 2027, unless a business chooses to comply early (which the government has urged, see Part 4).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 1 — Short title and commencement
body: The Act is cited as the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It comes into force on such date(s) as the Central Government notifies in the Official Gazette; different dates may be set for different provisions (used exactly this way — see phased timeline above).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 2 — Definitions
body:
Key defined terms (verbatim meaning preserved):
- **"Appellate Tribunal"** — the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), established under s.14 of the TRAI Act, 1997, designated as the appeal forum for DPDP Board orders.
- **"automated"** — any digital process capable of operating automatically in response to instructions, for processing data.
- **"Board"** — the Data Protection Board of India, established under Section 18.
- **"certain legitimate uses"** — the uses listed in Section 7.
- **"Chairperson"** — the Chairperson of the Board.
- **"child"** — an individual who has **not completed the age of 18 years**.
- **"Consent Manager"** — a person registered with the Board who acts as a single point of contact enabling a Data Principal to give, manage, review and withdraw consent through an accessible, transparent, interoperable platform.
- **"data"** — a representation of information, facts, concepts, opinions or instructions suitable for communication/interpretation/processing by humans or automated means.
- **"Data Fiduciary"** — any person who alone or with others determines the purpose and means of processing personal data (i.e., the "controller" in GDPR terms).
- **"Data Principal"** — the individual to whom the personal data relates; where the individual is a child, includes the parent/lawful guardian; where a person with disability, includes the lawful guardian acting on her behalf.
- **"Data Processor"** — any person processing personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary.
- **"Data Protection Officer"** — an individual appointed by a Significant Data Fiduciary under s.10(2)(a).
- **"digital office"** — an office running an online mechanism for the entire lifecycle of a proceeding (receipt to disposal).
- **"digital personal data"** — personal data in digital form (this is what the Act actually governs).
- **"gain"** / **"loss"** — defined broadly to include property, services, remuneration or financial-advantage effects (used in penalty determination under s.33(2)).
- **"person"** — includes an individual, HUF, company, firm, association of persons/body of individuals (incorporated or not), the State, and every other artificial juristic person.
- **"personal data"** — any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data.
- **"personal data breach"** — any unauthorised processing, or accidental disclosure/acquisition/sharing/use/alteration/destruction/loss of access to personal data compromising confidentiality, integrity or availability.
- **"processing"** — a wholly/partly automated operation on digital personal data, covering collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation, retrieval, use, combination, indexing, sharing, disclosure, dissemination, restriction, erasure, destruction.
- **"Significant Data Fiduciary" ("SDF")** — a Data Fiduciary/class notified as such by the Central Government under Section 10.
- **"State"** — as defined in Article 12 of the Constitution.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 3 — Application of Act
body: Applies to processing of digital personal data within India where data is (i) collected in digital form, or (ii) collected in non-digital form and later digitised. Also applies **extraterritorially** to processing outside India if it is in connection with offering goods/services to Data Principals within India. Does **not** apply to (a) personal data processed by an individual for personal/domestic purposes, or (b) personal data that is made publicly available by the Data Principal herself or by any person under a legal obligation to make it public (illustration given: a person blogging her own data publicly).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 4 — Grounds for processing of personal data
body: A person may process personal data of a Data Principal only per the Act and for a lawful purpose, either (a) with the Data Principal's consent, or (b) for "certain legitimate uses" under Section 7. "Lawful purpose" = any purpose not expressly forbidden by law.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 5 — Notice
body: Every consent request (under s.6) must be accompanied/preceded by a notice informing the Data Principal of: (i) the personal data and purpose of processing; (ii) how to exercise rights under s.6(4) (withdrawal) and s.13 (grievance redressal); (iii) how to complain to the Board. For **pre-Act consent** (i.e., consent obtained before commencement), the Data Fiduciary must, as soon as reasonably practicable, retrospectively give an equivalent notice; processing may continue until the Data Principal withdraws consent. Notice must be offered in English or any language listed in the **Eighth Schedule to the Constitution**.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 6 — Consent
body: Consent must be **free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous**, given via clear affirmative action, limited to data necessary for the specified purpose. Any part of a consent that infringes the Act/rules/other law is invalid *only to that extent* (illustration: a clause waiving the right to complain to the Board is invalid, rest of consent stands). Consent requests must be in clear/plain language, offered in a Schedule-8 language, with DPO/contact details. The Data Principal has an unconditional **right to withdraw consent at any time**, "with ease... comparable to the ease with which consent was given." Withdrawal does not retroactively invalidate prior processing; consequences of withdrawal are borne by the Data Principal (illustration: e-commerce order already placed can still be fulfilled). On withdrawal, the Fiduciary must, "within a reasonable time," cease (and cause its Processors to cease) processing, unless continued processing is otherwise legally required/authorised. Consent may be given/managed/withdrawn through a **Consent Manager**, who is accountable to the Data Principal and must be **registered with the Board** (s.6(9) — this registration duty commences at the one-year mark, ~Nov 2026). In any dispute, the **burden of proof is on the Data Fiduciary** to show that valid notice and consent were obtained (s.6(10)).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 7 — Certain legitimate uses

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 8 — General obligations of Data Fiduciary
body: The Fiduciary bears **non-delegable responsibility** for Act compliance even where a Data Processor does the actual processing, and irrespective of any contrary agreement or the Data Principal's own non-compliance. May engage a Processor only under a **valid contract**, for activities connected to offering goods/services. Where processed data will be used for a decision affecting the Data Principal, or disclosed to another Fiduciary, the Fiduciary must ensure **completeness, accuracy, and consistency**. Must implement "appropriate technical and organisational measures" and "reasonable security safeguards" to prevent breaches. On a **personal data breach**, must intimate **both the Board and each affected Data Principal**, in the prescribed form/manner (no statutory numeric deadline in the Act itself — the deadline detail is in the Rules, see Rule 7 below). Must **erase personal data** once consent is withdrawn or the specified purpose is no longer served (whichever earlier), unless retention is legally required, and must cause Processors to do the same. "No longer served" is deemed to occur if the Data Principal neither approaches the Fiduciary for the purpose nor exercises her rights, for a period to be prescribed (see Rule 8 / Third Schedule — the 3-year rule for large platforms). Must publish **DPO/grievance-contact business information**, and establish an **effective grievance redressal mechanism**.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 9 — Processing of personal data of children
body: Before processing a child's (or a disabled person's, where she has a lawful guardian) personal data, the Fiduciary must obtain **verifiable parental/guardian consent** in the prescribed manner. Must **not** process a child's data in a way likely to cause **detrimental effect on the child's well-being**. Must **not undertake tracking, behavioural monitoring, or targeted advertising directed at children**. The Central Government may prescribe exempt classes of Fiduciaries/purposes (implemented via Rule 12 / Fourth Schedule — e.g., healthcare providers, schools, crèches). The Central Government may also **notify a verifiably-safe Fiduciary's exemption above a certain age** if satisfied its processing is verifiably safe.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 10 — Additional obligations of Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF)
body: Central Government may notify any Fiduciary/class as an **SDF** based on factors: volume/sensitivity of data processed, risk to Data Principal rights, potential impact on India's sovereignty/integrity, risk to electoral democracy, security of the State, and public order. An SDF must: (a) appoint a **Data Protection Officer** — based in India, reporting to the Board of Directors, and the point of contact for grievance redressal; (b) appoint an **independent data auditor**; (c) undertake periodic **Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIA)**, periodic audits, and other prescribed measures.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 11 — Right to access information about personal data
body: A Data Principal may request from a Fiduciary to whom she gave consent: (a) a **summary** of her personal data being processed and the processing activities; (b) identities of **all other Fiduciaries/Processors** with whom her data has been shared, with a description of what was shared; (c) any other prescribed information. Exception: (b)/(c) do not apply where data was shared with another Fiduciary *authorised by law* pursuant to a written request for prevention/investigation/prosecution of offences or cyber incidents.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 12 — Right to correction and erasure of personal data
body: Right to **correction, completion, updating and erasure** of personal data for which she gave consent (subject to any other applicable legal procedure). On request, the Fiduciary must correct inaccurate/misleading data, complete incomplete data, and update it. On an **erasure** request, the Fiduciary must erase the data unless retention is necessary for the specified purpose or legal compliance.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 13 — Right of grievance redressal
body: Right to **readily available grievance redressal** from the Fiduciary or Consent Manager for any act/omission regarding obligations or the Data Principal's rights. The Fiduciary/Consent Manager must respond within a **prescribed period** (set at 90 days by Rule 14(3), see below). The Data Principal must **exhaust this grievance route before approaching the Board**.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 14 — Right to nominate
body: Right to **nominate another individual**, in the prescribed manner, to exercise her rights in the event of her **death or incapacity**. "Incapacity" = inability to exercise rights due to unsoundness of mind or bodily infirmity.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 15 — Duties of Data Principal
body: The Data Principal must: (a) comply with all applicable laws when exercising Act rights; (b) **not impersonate** another person when providing personal data; (c) **not suppress material information** when providing data for a State-issued document/identifier/proof of identity/address; (d) **not register false or frivolous grievances/complaints**; (e) furnish only **verifiably authentic information** when exercising correction/erasure rights. (Breach of these duties is itself a penalty ground under the Schedule — up to ₹10,000.)

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 16 — Processing of personal data outside India
body: The Central Government may, by notification, **restrict transfer** of personal data to specific countries/territories outside India (a "blacklist" model rather than the EU's adequacy/whitelist model). Does not override any other Indian law providing a *higher* degree of protection/restriction on cross-border transfer.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 17 — Exemptions
body: Chapter II (except s.8(1) and (5)), Chapter III, and Section 16 **do not apply** where processing is necessary for: (a) enforcing a legal right/claim; (b) court/tribunal/regulatory or quasi-judicial functions; (c) prevention/detection/investigation/prosecution of offences; (d) processing of data of persons outside India pursuant to a contract with a person outside India (by an India-based processor); (e) a court/tribunal-approved scheme of merger/amalgamation/demerger; (f) ascertaining a loan defaulter's financial position (per Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code definitions). The **entire Act** is disapplied for: (a) processing by a notified State instrumentality in the interests of sovereignty/security/public order (and the Central Government's processing of data furnished by such instrumentality); (b) processing for **research, archiving, or statistical purposes**, provided it meets prescribed standards (implemented via Rule 16 / Second Schedule) and is not used for individual-specific decisions. The Central Government may also **exempt certain classes of Fiduciaries (including startups)** from ss.5, 8(3), 8(7), 10 and 11, having regard to volume/nature of data processed. For State processing, s.8(7) (erasure duty) and s.12(3) (erasure right) don't apply, and s.12(2) (correction) doesn't apply where the purpose excludes individual-specific decisions. The Central Government may, **within 5 years of commencement**, notify further temporary exemptions for any Fiduciary/class.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 18 — Establishment of Board
body: Establishes the **Data Protection Board of India**, effective from a notified date (in force since 13/14 Nov 2025). It is a **body corporate** with perpetual succession, a common seal, and power to acquire/hold/dispose of property and to sue/be sued. Headquarters at a Central-Government-notified place (reported as the National Capital Region / New Delhi).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 19 — Composition and qualifications for appointment of Chairperson and Members
body: Board = Chairperson + notified number of other Members. Appointed by the Central Government in the prescribed manner (see Rule 17 below). Must be persons of **ability, integrity and standing** with special knowledge/practical experience in data governance, social/consumer-protection law administration, dispute resolution, ICT, digital economy, law/regulation/techno-regulation, or any other field the Government finds useful — **at least one Member must be a law expert**.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 20 — Salary, allowances payable to and term of office
body: Salary/allowances/service conditions as prescribed (see Fifth Schedule to the Rules: ₹4.5 lakh/month for Chairperson, ₹4 lakh/month for other Members, no house/car). Cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment. **Term: 2 years**, eligible for re-appointment.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 21 — Disqualifications for appointment and continuation as Chairperson and Members
body: Disqualified if: (a) adjudged insolvent; (b) convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude; (c) physically/mentally incapacitated; (d) has a prejudicial financial/other interest; (e) has abused position prejudicially. Removal requires an **opportunity of being heard**.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 22 — Resignation by Members and filling of vacancy
body: Resignation effective on the earliest of: Government-permitted relinquishment date, expiry of 3 months' notice, a successor taking office, or term expiry. Vacancies filled by fresh appointment. **Post-tenure cooling-off**: for 1 year after ceasing office, a Chairperson/Member cannot accept employment without prior Central Government approval, and must disclose any subsequent employment with a Fiduciary against whom they handled proceedings.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 23 — Proceedings of Board
body: Board sets its own meeting/business-transaction procedure (including digital means) and authentication method for orders/directions, as prescribed. **No Board act/proceeding is invalidated merely by**: a vacancy/defect in constitution, a defect in appointment, or a procedural irregularity not affecting merits. If the Chairperson cannot function (absence/illness/other cause), the **senior-most Member** acts until she resumes.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 24 — Officers and employees of Board
body: Board may, with prior Central Government approval, appoint officers/employees as needed, on prescribed terms.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 25 — Members and officers to be public servants
body: Chairperson, Members, officers and employees are deemed **"public servants"** under Section 21 of the Indian Penal Code when acting under the Act.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 26 — Powers of Chairperson
body: Chairperson exercises: (a) general superintendence/direction over administrative matters; (b) authorising any officer to scrutinise intimations/complaints/references/correspondence; (c) authorising individual Members/groups of Members to perform Board functions and allocating proceedings among them.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 27 — Powers and functions of Board
body: The Board's core jurisdictional triggers: (a) on receiving a **personal data breach intimation** under s.8(6), directing urgent remedial/mitigation measures, inquiring, and imposing penalties; (b) on a **Data Principal's complaint** about a breach or Fiduciary's obligation/rights violation, or a Central/State Government reference, or a court direction — inquire and penalise; (c) on a **complaint about a Consent Manager's** obligation breach — inquire and penalise; (d) on **intimation of breach of a Consent Manager's registration conditions** — inquire and penalise (this clause commences at the one-year mark, ~Nov 2026); (e) on a **Central Government reference re: an intermediary's breach of s.37(2)** (blocking-order non-compliance) — inquire and penalise. The Board may, after a hearing and recorded reasons, issue **binding directions**, and may modify/suspend/withdraw/cancel a direction on representation or Government reference.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 28 — Procedure to be followed by Board
body: The Board functions as an **independent body** and, as far as practicable, a **digital office** (digital-by-design complaint receipt, hearing, decision). It determines whether there are **sufficient grounds to proceed**; if insufficient, it may close the case (with recorded reasons); if sufficient, it inquires following **principles of natural justice**, recording reasons throughout. For inquiries, the Board has the **same powers as a civil court under the CPC, 1908** — summoning/enforcing attendance and examining on oath, receiving affidavit evidence, requiring document production, inspecting data/books/registers. The Board/its officers **cannot prevent access to premises or seize equipment** that would adversely affect day-to-day functioning. May requisition police/government officer assistance. May issue **interim orders** during inquiry (after hearing). On completion (after hearing), may close the proceeding or proceed to penalty under Section 33. If, at any stage, a complaint appears **false or frivolous**, the Board may warn or impose costs on the complainant.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 29 — Appeal to Appellate Tribunal
body: Any person aggrieved by a Board order/direction may appeal to the **Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT)** within **60 days** of receipt (condonable for sufficient cause), in the prescribed form/manner/fee. The Tribunal, after hearing both parties, may confirm/modify/set aside the order, and must send a copy to the Board and parties. Appeals should be disposed of **"as expeditiously as possible," with an endeavour to finish within 6 months**; if not, reasons must be recorded in writing. The Tribunal functions **digital-by-design** too.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 30 — Orders passed by Appellate Tribunal to be executable as decree
body: A Tribunal order is executable as a **civil court decree**, with the Tribunal having all civil-court powers for this purpose; alternatively it may transmit the order to a local civil court for execution.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 31 — Alternate dispute resolution
body: If the Board considers a complaint suitable for **mediation**, it may direct the parties to attempt resolution via a mutually-agreed mediator or one under existing law.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 32 — Voluntary undertaking
body: The Board may accept a **voluntary undertaking** from a person at any inquiry stage (s.28), including an undertaking to take/refrain from specified action within a set time, or to publicise the undertaking. Terms may be varied with the person's consent. Acceptance **bars further proceedings** on the undertaking's contents — *unless* the person later breaches a term, in which case it is deemed an Act breach and the Board may proceed to penalty under Section 33 (after a hearing).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 33 — Penalties
body: If the Board concludes, after an inquiry, that a breach is **"significant,"** it may (after a hearing) impose a **monetary penalty as specified in the Schedule** (see table below). In fixing the amount, the Board must have regard to: (a) nature/gravity/duration of breach; (b) type/nature of personal data affected; (c) whether the breach is repetitive; (d) whether the person gained or avoided a loss from the breach; (e) mitigation actions taken and their timeliness/effectiveness; (f) proportionality/deterrent effect of the penalty; (g) likely impact of the penalty on the person.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 34 — Crediting sums realised by way of penalties to Consolidated Fund of India
body: All penalty sums go to the **Consolidated Fund of India** (not retained by the Board or paid to complainants).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 35 — Protection of action taken in good faith
body: No suit/prosecution/legal proceeding lies against the Central Government, the Board, Chairperson, or any Member/officer/employee for anything done **in good faith** under the Act/rules.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 36 — Power to call for information
body: The Central Government may require the **Board** and any **Data Fiduciary or intermediary** to furnish information it calls for.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 37 — Power of Central Government to issue directions
body: Where the Board has, in **two or more instances**, imposed a monetary penalty on a Fiduciary, and advises (in the public interest) blocking public access to information enabling that Fiduciary's India-facing activity, the Central Government (or a specially authorised officer), after hearing the Fiduciary and recording reasons, may **direct any government agency or intermediary to block public access** to that information. Every intermediary receiving such a direction must comply. "Computer resource," "information," "intermediary" take their meaning from the **Information Technology Act, 2000**. (This is the Act's website/app-blocking power — a significant enforcement tool, notable for a compliance chatbot to flag as high-severity.)

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 38 — Consistency with other laws
body: The Act is **in addition to, not in derogation of**, any other law. Where the Act **conflicts** with another law, the **DPDP Act prevails** to the extent of the conflict.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 39 — Bar of jurisdiction
body: **No civil court** may entertain a suit/proceeding over a matter the Board is empowered to decide; **no court/authority may grant an injunction** in respect of any action taken/to be taken under the Act.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 40 — Power to make rules
body: Central Government may make rules (by notification, subject to prior publication) not inconsistent with the Act, covering an extensive list of matters (sub-clauses (a)–(z)) — essentially every "as may be prescribed" reference across the Act (notice manner, Consent Manager registration/accountability, subsidy/benefit processing categories, breach-intimation form, retention-deemed-served time period, DPO contact publication manner, verifiable child consent manner, child-processing exempt classes, DPIA process, SDF measures, Data Principal request manner, nomination manner, grievance-response period, Board Chairperson/Member appointment manner and service conditions, Board authentication/digital-office measures, appeal form/fee/procedure, etc.). This is the enabling provision under which the **DPDP Rules, 2025** (Part 2 below) were made.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 41 — Laying of rules and certain notifications
body: Every rule made, and every notification issued under Sections 16 and 42, must be **laid before both Houses of Parliament** for a total of 30 days (in one or more sessions); Parliament may modify or annul it (without prejudicing prior action taken under it).

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 42 — Power to amend Schedule
body: Central Government may, by notification, **amend the penalty Schedule** — but a notification **cannot more than double** any penalty figure as originally enacted. Any such amendment takes effect from the notification date, as if originally enacted.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 43 — Power to remove difficulties
body: If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the Act, the Central Government may, by Gazette order, make necessary provisions not inconsistent with the Act — but **no such order after 3 years from commencement**. Every such order must be laid before Parliament.

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: Section 44 — Amendments to certain Acts
body:
(1) Amends **Section 14(c) of the TRAI Act, 1997** to add the DPDP Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) as one of the tribunals TDSAT subsumes/serves.
(2) Amends the **Information Technology Act, 2000**: (a) **omits Section 43A** (the IT Act's existing "compensation for failure to protect data" provision — effectively superseded by the DPDP Act's penalty regime); (b) inserts a DPDP Act cross-reference into the s.81 proviso (IT Act to have effect notwithstanding other laws, except Patents Act and now DPDP Act); (c) omits s.87(2)(ob) (rule-making power for the reasonable-security-practices rules under old s.43A, now redundant).
(3) Amends **Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005**: replaces the earlier exemption (personal information causing unwarranted invasion of privacy, subject to a public-interest override and a "cannot deny to Parliament/Legislature" proviso) with a **blanket exemption for "information which relates to personal information."** This is one of the most consequential and debated changes in the Act — it **removes the public-interest-override balancing test** that previously existed in RTI cases involving personal data, making essentially all "personal information" categorically exempt from RTI disclosure regardless of countervailing public interest. (See Part 4 for further context — this amendment is itself commenced already, from 13/14 Nov 2025, since s.44(1)/(3) are in the first commencement tranche; s.44(2) — the IT Act amendments — is deferred to the 18-month/May-2027 tranche.)

part: PART 1 — THE DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION ACT, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
heading: THE SCHEDULE — Penalties [see Section 33(1)]
body:
| Sl. No. | Breach | Penalty (may extend to) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Breach of the Fiduciary's obligation to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach (s.8(5)) | **₹250 crore** |
| 2 | Breach of the obligation to give the Board/affected Data Principal notice of a personal data breach (s.8(6)) | **₹200 crore** |
| 3 | Breach of additional obligations relating to children (s.9) | **₹200 crore** |
| 4 | Breach of additional obligations of a Significant Data Fiduciary (s.10) | **₹150 crore** |
| 5 | Breach of the duties of a Data Principal (s.15) | **₹10,000** |
| 6 | Breach of any term of a voluntary undertaking accepted by the Board (s.32) | Up to the extent applicable to the breach for which s.28 proceedings were originally instituted |
| 7 | Breach of any other provision of the Act or rules | **₹50 crore** |

(All figures are statutory ceilings — "may extend to" — not fixed/mandatory amounts; the Board sets the actual figure per the s.33(2) factors above. Note the asymmetry: penalties on Data Fiduciaries range up to ₹250 crore, while the only penalty specifically on a **Data Principal** — for breach of duties under s.15 — is capped at a comparatively nominal ₹10,000.)

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Status (as verified from primary sources)
body:
**FINALLY NOTIFIED — not draft.** The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were **notified via Gazette Notification G.S.R. 846(E), dated 13 November 2025** (Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II—Section 3, Sub-section (i), No. 760), under powers conferred by Section 40(1) and (2) of the DPDP Act. Signed by **Ajit Kumar, Joint Secretary**, MeitY. Official PIB explainer (17 Nov 2025) describes this as the date the Rules "give full effect to" the DPDP Act; some secondary/press sources describe the effective date as **14 November 2025** (see Key Uncertainties re: the one-day discrepancy between the gazette's own dateline of 13 Nov and press description of 14 Nov).

**History:** A **draft** of these Rules was first published for public consultation on **3 January 2025** (G.S.R. 02(E)), with a 45-day comment window (closing ~18 February 2025, later effectively extended in practice). MeitY held in-person consultations in **Delhi, Mumbai, Guwahati, Kolkata, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai**, and received **6,915 inputs** in total from startups, MSMEs, industry bodies, civil society and citizens before finalising. The gap between draft (Jan 2025) and final notification (Nov 2025) was about **10 months**. Compared to the draft, the notified final Rules made at least two substantive additions flagged by legal commentary (Bar & Bench/S.S. Rana & Co., cross-checked against the Rules text itself, which was independently verified in this research): (i) a stronger localisation restriction for Significant Data Fiduciaries in Rule 13(4) (specified personal data and its associated traffic data must not be transferred outside India, based on a government committee's recommendations); and (ii) the new Rule 13(5) defining that "committee" (MeitY officials, possibly joined by other ministries/departments).

**No further amendment to these Rules has been identified as of the compilation date** (27 September 2026) beyond the original notification — see Key Uncertainties for the limits of this research's ability to detect a very recent amendment.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Commencement schedule of the Rules (Rule 1)
body:
The Rules do **not** all commence together — this is important for a compliance chatbot to get right:
- **Rules 1, 2, and 17–21** (short title/definitions, and the Board's constitution/procedure/staffing rules) — in force **from the date of gazette publication** (13/14 Nov 2025).
- **Rule 4** (Consent Manager registration and obligations) — in force **one year after publication**, i.e., ~13/14 **November 2026**.
- **Rules 3, 5–16, 22 and 23** (notice content, subsidy-processing standards, security safeguards, breach intimation, erasure timelines, children's/disability consent, SDF obligations, Data Principal rights mechanics, cross-border transfer, research exemption, Tribunal appeal mechanics, information-calling power) — in force **eighteen months after publication**, i.e., ~13/14 **May 2027**.

This mirrors the Act's own three-phase commencement (Part 1 above) almost exactly — the Rules simply operationalise whichever Act provisions are live at each phase.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 1 — Short title and commencement
body: Cited as the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025. Commencement is staggered as described above.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 2 — Definitions
body: Defines "Act" (the DPDP Act, 2023); "techno-legal measures" (per Rules 20 and 22 — the Board/Tribunal's digital-office mechanisms); "user account" (a Data Principal's online account with a Fiduciary, including profiles/pages/handles/email/mobile number and similar presences); "verifiable consent" (as specified in Rule 10 or 11). Undefined terms take their meaning from the Act.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 3 — Notice given by Data Fiduciary to Data Principal
body: The notice must: (a) be presented and understandable **independently** of any other information the Fiduciary has made/may make available (i.e., cannot be buried in a long privacy policy — must stand alone); (b) in clear/plain language, give a fair account sufficient for specific/informed consent, including **at minimum** an itemised description of the personal data and the specified purpose(s)/goods/services enabled; (c) give the specific communication link to access the Fiduciary's website/app, and describe other means by which the Data Principal may withdraw consent (with ease comparable to giving it), exercise Act rights, and complain to the Board.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 4 — Registration and obligations of Consent Manager
body: *(Commences ~Nov 2026.)* A person meeting **Part A of the First Schedule** conditions may apply to the Board for registration, furnishing particulars the Board publishes on its website. The Board may inquire and either (a) register + publish the Consent Manager's particulars, or (b) reject with reasons. Obligations are set out in **Part B of the First Schedule**. If the Board finds non-adherence, it may (after a hearing) direct corrective measures; if satisfied it is necessary in Data Principals' interests, it may (after a hearing, with written reasons) **suspend or cancel registration** and issue protective directions. The Board may demand information from a Consent Manager at any time.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 5 — Processing of personal data for provision or issue of subsidy, benefit, service, certificate, licence or permit by State and its instrumentalities
body: Implements s.7(b) of the Act. Processing must follow the **Second Schedule** standards. Clarifies that "under law"/"under policy"/"using public funds" references cover, respectively: statutory/executive powers of the State; Central/State Government policy or executive instructions; and expenditure from/receipts accruing to the Consolidated Fund of India/State, public account of India/State, or local/other authority funds.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 6 — Reasonable security safeguards
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.8(5). At minimum, a Data Fiduciary must adopt: (a) data security measures such as **encryption, obfuscation, masking, or virtual tokens**; (b) access-control measures for computer resources; (c) **logging, monitoring and review** for visibility into access (to detect/investigate/remediate unauthorised access); (d) reasonable continuity measures (e.g., **data backups**) in the event confidentiality/integrity/availability is compromised; (e) **retention of logs and personal data for a minimum of one year** (unless law requires otherwise) to enable detection/investigation/remediation; (f) appropriate contractual security provisions with Data Processors; (g) appropriate technical/organisational measures generally. "Computer resource" takes the IT Act, 2000 meaning.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 7 — Intimation of personal data breach
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* On becoming aware of a breach, the Fiduciary must, **without delay**, notify each affected Data Principal (via her user account or registered communication channel), in concise/clear/plain language, covering: (a) description of the breach (nature, extent, timing); (b) relevant consequences for her; (c) mitigation measures implemented/being implemented; (d) safety measures she may take; (e) business contact info for queries. Separately, the Fiduciary must notify **the Board**: (a) **without delay**, a description (nature, extent, timing, location, likely impact); (b) **within 72 hours of becoming aware** (or a longer period the Board allows on written request), a fuller report covering updated/detailed information, facts/circumstances/causes, mitigation measures, findings on the person who caused the breach, remedial measures to prevent recurrence, and a report on intimations given to affected Data Principals. **This 72-hour Board-notification deadline is one of the single most operationally important numbers in the entire framework for a compliance chatbot to surface accurately** — note that the Act itself (s.8(6)) does not specify a number; the 72-hour figure comes from this Rule.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 8 — Time period for specified purpose to be deemed as no longer being served
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.8(8). A Fiduciary of a class specified in the **Third Schedule**, processing for corresponding purposes, must erase personal data unless retention is legally required, or — for the Third-Schedule time period — if the Data Principal neither approaches the Fiduciary for the purpose nor exercises her rights. At least **48 hours before** the erasure deadline, the Fiduciary must warn the Data Principal that data will be erased unless she logs in / contacts the Fiduciary / exercises her rights. **Independently of the above**, a Fiduciary must retain personal data, associated traffic data, and processing logs for a **minimum of one year from the date of processing** for the purposes in the **Seventh Schedule**, after which it must be erased (unless further retention is legally required/notified). Illustrations given: an e-book platform must keep order/payment/delivery logs for ≥1 year from the transaction even if the user deletes her account; a company using a cloud processor must ensure the processor also retains data/logs for ≥1 year before erasure.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 9 — Contact information of person to answer questions about processing
body: Every Fiduciary must prominently publish (website/app) and mention in every rights-related response, the business contact info of the **DPO (if applicable) or another responsible person**.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 10 — Verifiable consent for processing of personal data of child
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Fiduciary must adopt appropriate technical/organisational measures to obtain **verifiable parental consent** before processing a child's data, and exercise **due diligence** to confirm the self-identified parent is an identifiable adult, by reference to: (a) reliable identity/age details already held; or (b) identity/age details voluntarily provided by the individual, or via a **virtual token** issued by an "authorised entity" (a government-designated identity/age-verification body, or a **Digital Locker service provider**). "Adult" = completed 18 years. Four detailed illustrations are given (child self-declares parent who is/isn't already a registered user; parent opens the account and is/isn't already registered) — in each case, the Fiduciary must independently verify the parent's identity/age via reliable records or an authorised-entity/DigiLocker token, not merely take the child's or parent's word for it.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 11 — Verifiable consent for processing of personal data of person with disability who has lawful guardian
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Fiduciary must exercise due diligence to verify that a self-identified "lawful guardian" of a person with disability was **actually appointed by a court, a designated authority (under s.15, Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016), or a local-level committee** (under the National Trust Act, 1999) — not merely accept a self-declaration. Defines "person with disability" by reference to the RPwD Act, 2016 and National Trust Act, 1999 definitions (including autism, cerebral palsy, mental retardation, severe multiple disability, and general long-term impairment categories where the person cannot take legally binding decisions despite adequate support).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 12 — Exemptions from certain obligations applicable to processing of personal data of child
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.9(4). Section 9(1) and (3) (verifiable consent + no tracking/behavioural monitoring/targeted ads) **do not apply** to: **Part A** — specified classes of Fiduciaries (clinical/mental-health establishments and healthcare professionals — for health-service processing; allied healthcare professionals — for implementing referral/treatment plans; educational institutions — for tracking/monitoring tied to educational activities or child safety; crèche/daycare individual caregivers — for safety-related tracking; transport providers engaged by schools/crèches — for location-tracking during transit), each subject to the stated conditions; **Part B** — specified purposes regardless of Fiduciary type (exercising a legal power/function/duty in a child's interest; providing a government subsidy/benefit/service/licence/permit in the child's interest; creating an email-communication-only user account; determining a child's **real-time location** for safety; blocking access to content/services/ads likely to harm the child's well-being; and the Fiduciary's own age-verification/due-diligence process under Rule 10), each restricted to what is "necessary" for that purpose.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 13 — Additional obligations of Significant Data Fiduciary
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.10(2)(c). An SDF must, **once every 12 months** from the date of SDF notification, undertake a **Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and an audit**, and cause the assessor/auditor to submit a report of significant observations to the **Board**. Must exercise due diligence that its technical measures (including **algorithmic software**) for hosting/display/upload/modification/publishing/transmission/storage/updating/sharing of personal data are not likely to risk Data Principals' rights. Must ensure that personal data **specified by the Central Government** (on recommendation of a constituted committee) — together with associated **traffic data** — is **not transferred outside India's territory** (this is the notable data-localisation addition versus the January 2025 draft). The "committee" = MeitY officials, possibly joined by other ministries/departments.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 14 — Rights of Data Principals
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Fiduciary/Consent Manager must prominently publish (website/app) the means of making a rights-request and any identifying particulars (e.g., username) needed. A Data Principal exercises rights by requesting the Fiduciary to whom she gave consent, via the specified means. Every Fiduciary/Consent Manager must publish, and implement measures to meet, a **grievance-redressal response period of no more than 90 days**. A Data Principal may **nominate** one or more individuals per the Fiduciary's terms of service. "Identifier" is defined broadly (customer ID file number, application reference number, enrolment ID, email, mobile number, licence number, etc.).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 15 — Transfer of personal data outside the territory of India
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.16. Personal data may be transferred outside India, subject to any requirements the Central Government specifies (by general/special order) regarding making such data available to a **foreign State or a person/entity/agency under its control**. (Note: unlike GDPR-style adequacy assessments, the Rules as notified do not establish a whitelist/blacklist of countries — this is left to future government orders; no such order has been identified as issued yet — flagged in Key Uncertainties.)

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 16 — Exemption from Act for research, archiving or statistical purposes
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.17(2)(b). The Act does not apply to such processing if it meets the **Second Schedule** standards (same standards schedule as Rule 5).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 17 — Appointment of Chairperson and other Members
body: *(In force since Nov 2025.)* Two **Search-cum-Selection Committees**: (1) for the **Chairperson** — chaired by the **Cabinet Secretary**, with the Secretaries in charge of the Department of Legal Affairs and MeitY, plus two subject-matter experts, as members; (2) for **other Members** — chaired by the **MeitY Secretary**, with the Secretary in charge of Legal Affairs, plus two experts. The Central Government appoints after considering the Committee's recommended candidates. No Committee action is invalidated merely for a vacancy/absence/constitutional defect.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 18 — Salary, allowances and other terms and conditions of service of Chairperson and other Members
body: Per the **Fifth Schedule** (see below).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 19 — Procedure for meetings of Board and authentication of its orders, directions and instruments
body: *(In force since Nov 2025.)* Chairperson fixes meeting date/time/place and agenda. Meetings chaired by the Chairperson (or, in her absence, a Member chosen by those present). **Quorum: one-third of Board membership.** Decisions by majority of Members present and voting; Chairperson (or presiding Member) has a **casting vote** on a tie. A Member with a personal interest in an agenda item must recuse from participating/voting on it. In an **emergency**, the Chairperson may act unilaterally (with written reasons), reporting to all Members within 7 days and placing it before the Board for ratification at its next meeting. Business may also be decided by **circulation** among Members if the Chairperson so directs. Orders/directions/instruments are authenticated by signature of the Chairperson, a Member, or an authorised individual. **Board inquiries must be completed within 6 months** of receiving the intimation/complaint/reference/direction under s.27, extendable in further tranches of **not more than 3 months at a time** (with recorded reasons).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 20 — Functioning of Board as digital office
body: *(In force since Nov 2025.)* The Board functions as a digital office and may adopt techno-legal measures to conduct proceedings without requiring physical presence — without prejudice to its power to summon/enforce attendance and examine on oath.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 21 — Terms and conditions of appointment and service of officers and employees of Board
body: *(In force since Nov 2025.)* Board may, with prior Central Government approval, appoint officers/employees as needed. Terms per the **Sixth Schedule**.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 22 — Appeal to Appellate Tribunal
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Appeals against Board orders/directions go to the Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT), filed **digitally** as the Tribunal decides. Appeal fee = **same as TRAI Act, 1997 appeal fees**, unless reduced/waived by the Tribunal Chairperson's discretion; payable digitally via **UPI or an RBI-authorised payment system**. The Tribunal is **not bound by CPC, 1908 procedure**, is guided by natural justice, may regulate its own procedure, and functions as a digital office (same non-physical-presence approach as the Board, without prejudice to summoning powers).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Rule 23 — Calling for information from Data Fiduciary or intermediary
body: *(Commences ~May 2027.)* Implements s.36 read with the **Seventh Schedule**. For the Seventh-Schedule purposes, the Central Government (acting through the Schedule's specified "authorised person") may require a Fiduciary/intermediary to furnish information within a specified period. Where disclosure could prejudice India's sovereignty/integrity/State security, the Government may bar the Fiduciary/intermediary from telling the affected Data Principal or anyone else, absent the authorised person's prior written permission. "Intermediary" takes the IT Act, 2000 meaning.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: First Schedule — Consent Manager conditions and obligations [Rule 4]
body:
**Part A (registration conditions):** applicant must be (1) a company incorporated in India; (2) possess sufficient technical/operational/financial capacity; (3) have sound financial condition and management; (4) have **net worth ≥ ₹2 crore**; (5) have adequate business volume/capital structure/earning prospects; (6) have directors/KMPs/senior management of good general reputation, fairness and integrity; (7) have MOA/AOA provisions requiring adherence to Part B items 9–10, amendable only with prior Board approval; (8) propose operations in Data Principals' interest; (9) be independently certified that its interoperable consent platform meets Board-published data-protection standards, with appropriate technical/organisational measures in place.

**Part B (ongoing obligations):** must (1) enable Data Principals to give consent directly to an onboarded Fiduciary or via another onboarded Fiduciary holding the data; (2) ensure data shared/made-available through it is **not readable by the Consent Manager itself**; (3) maintain records of consents given/denied/withdrawn, notices, and data-sharing events; (4) give Data Principals access to those records, provide them in **machine-readable form** on request, and **retain records for ≥7 years** (or longer as agreed/required by law); (5) maintain a website/app as the primary access channel; (6) **not sub-contract or assign** its obligations; (7) take reasonable security safeguards against breaches; (8) act in a **fiduciary capacity** toward the Data Principal; (9)–(10) avoid conflicts of interest with Data Fiduciaries (including via directors'/KMPs' financial interests, directorships, employment, or beneficial ownership); (11) publish (website/app) details of its promoters/directors/KMPs/senior management, any >2% shareholders, any corporate in which its own promoters/directors/KMPs/senior management hold >2%, and any other Board-directed transparency disclosures; (12) maintain effective **audit mechanisms** reporting to the Board periodically (and on demand) covering technical/organisational controls, continued registration-condition compliance, and Act/Rules adherence; (13) **not transfer control** (sale/merger/otherwise) without prior Board approval and compliance with Board-specified conditions.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Second Schedule — Standards for State-instrumentality processing under s.7(b) and for research/archiving/statistical exemption under s.17(2)(b) [Rules 5(1), 16]
body: Requires appropriate technical/organisational measures ensuring: lawful processing; processing limited to the s.7(b)/s.17(2)(b) uses/purposes; data limited to what's necessary; reasonable efforts at completeness/accuracy/consistency; retention only as long as necessary/legally required; reasonable security safeguards against breach; (for s.7(b) processing specifically) intimation to the Data Principal with DPO/contact info and a communication link for exercising rights, consistent with any government policy/law; and accountability of whoever determines purpose/means of the processing.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Third Schedule — Deemed-erasure classes, purposes and time periods [Rule 8(1)]
body:
Three specified classes, each with a **3-year** erasure trigger (from last Data-Principal contact for the purpose/rights exercise, or from the Rules' commencement, whichever is **latest**), covering "all purposes" **except** enabling account access and virtual-token access for money/goods/services:
1. **E-commerce entity with ≥2 crore registered users in India.**
2. **Online gaming intermediary with ≥50 lakh registered users in India.**
3. **Social media intermediary with ≥2 crore registered users in India.**

Definitions cross-reference the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (e-commerce entity — excludes marketplace sellers) and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (social media intermediary).

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Fourth Schedule — Children's-data exemptions [Rule 12]
body:
**Part A** (exempt Fiduciary classes + conditions): clinical/mental-health establishments and healthcare professionals (health-service-necessary processing only); allied healthcare professionals (treatment/referral-plan support only); educational institutions (tracking/monitoring for educational activities or child safety only); crèche/daycare individual caregivers (safety-related tracking only); transport providers for schools/crèches (location-tracking during transit only).
**Part B** (exempt purposes regardless of Fiduciary): legal power/function/duty in a child's interest; government subsidy/benefit/service/licence/permit in a child's interest; email-only account creation; real-time location determination for child safety; blocking harmful content/services/ads from reaching the child; the Fiduciary's own age-verification due diligence under Rule 10 — each restricted to what's "necessary."

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Fifth Schedule — Chairperson/Member service terms [Rule 18]
body: **Salary:** Chairperson ₹4,50,000/month; other Members ₹4,00,000/month (both **without house or car facility**). Eligible to contribute to the Board's Provident Fund; **not entitled to pension or gratuity** for Board service. Travel allowance at Pay Matrix **Level 17** (Chairperson) / **Level 15** (other Members) rates; foreign travel only per Central Government guidelines. Medical assistance under the Board's group health insurance scheme (or, for retirees from government/PSU service, an opt-in to their prior service's medical rules). Leave per specified Central Civil Services (Leave) Rules, 1972 provisions, with earned-leave encashment capped at **50%** of standing credit (except under CCS Rule 38-A). Leave Travel Concession per CCS (LTC) Rules, 1988, with a home-town-or-anywhere-in-India choice every 2 years. Must avoid conflicts of interest; CCS (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1965 Parts IV–IX apply mutatis mutandis; **no sitting fees or sumptuary allowance**. Unaddressed service matters go to the Central Government for final decision.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Sixth Schedule — Officer/employee service terms [Rule 21(2)]
body: Board may appoint officers/employees on **deputation** (from Central/State Government, autonomous bodies, statutory bodies, PSUs) for up to **5 years**, per Fundamental Rules and DoPT guidelines; may also take on deputation from the **National Institute for Smart Government** for up to 5 years, at market-standard salary. Gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. Travel allowance/leave/LTC per standard Central Government officer terms. Civil Service (Conduct) Rules, 1964 and CCS (CCA) Rules, 1965 Parts IV–IX apply mutatis mutandis. Unaddressed matters go to the Central Government for final decision.

part: PART 2 — DIGITAL PERSONAL DATA PROTECTION RULES, 2025
heading: Seventh Schedule — Information-calling purposes and authorised persons [Rules 23(1), 8(3)]
body:
Three specified purposes, each with a designated "authorised person":
1. **State/instrumentality use of personal data in the interest of sovereignty/integrity/security of India** — authorised person = the officer designated under s.17(2)(a) of the Act by the Central Government or the instrumentality's head.
2. **State/instrumentality use for performing a legal function, or disclosing information to fulfil a legal obligation** — authorised person = whoever is authorised under the applicable law.
3. **Carrying out the assessment for notifying a Fiduciary/class as a Significant Data Fiduciary** — authorised person = an officer designated by the MeitY Secretary.

(This Seventh Schedule is also cross-referenced by Rule 8(3) as defining the purposes for which the 1-year minimum log/traffic-data retention applies.)

part: PART 3 — MEITY OFFICIAL FAQs ON THE DPDP ACT, 2023
heading: Official MeitY FAQ: none found (verification note)
body:
**Finding: No official, MeitY-published FAQ document specifically on the DPDP Act, 2023 (or the DPDP Rules, 2025) could be located and verified in this research, despite an extensive targeted search of meity.gov.in and pib.gov.in.**

What was checked and ruled out:
- A PDF titled *"FAQs – The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023"* is circulating online (e.g., hosted at cyrilshroff.com), but on direct inspection this is explicitly labelled **"a thought leadership initiative"** of the law firm **Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas**, dated December 2025, with an explicit disclaimer that it "does not constitute legal advice" and is **not** an official government publication. It should **not** be presented to end users as a MeitY document.
- A genuine MeitY "Frequently Asked Questions" PDF was found at `meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/10/...pdf`, but it concerns the unrelated **Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026** (on synthetically-generated information/deepfakes), dated 10 February 2026 — not the DPDP Act.
- The MeitY page `meity.gov.in/content/digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023` (which likely hosts the Act, Rules, and possibly a FAQ/explainer link) returned an HTTP 403 to this session's automated fetch tool and could not be directly inspected; it is plausible an official FAQ or explanatory note exists there or elsewhere on meity.gov.in that this research could not access. **The lawyer using this chatbot should manually check `meity.gov.in/content/digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023` and the MeitY "Data Protection Framework" section for an FAQ PDF before concluding none exists.**
- The official PIB explainer document (`doc20251117695301.pdf`, dated 17 Nov 2025, cited throughout Part 1–2 above) is *not* structured as Q&A, but it is an authentic, official plain-language explainer covering: the Act's "SARAL" (Simple, Accessible, Rational, Actionable) design philosophy; the 7 core data-protection principles (consent & transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security safeguards, accountability); key term definitions; penalty figures; a rights summary; and — notably — an explanation of how the DPDP Act's RTI amendment (s.44(3), see Part 1 above) interacts with the **Puttaswamy** privacy judgment and RTI Act s.8(2)'s public-interest override. This document is the closest official analogue to an "FAQ" and its content has been fully incorporated into Parts 1, 2 and 4 of this knowledge base.

**Recommendation for the chatbot:** until an official MeitY FAQ is independently located, the chatbot should **not** cite any "MeitY FAQ" as a source, and should instead answer FAQ-style questions by drawing directly on the Act/Rules text (Parts 1–2) and the official PIB explainer (cited above), making clear these are primary-source-derived answers rather than quotes from an official Q&A document.

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.1 Data Protection Board of India — real-world operational status
body:
- **Legal establishment:** live since 13/14 November 2025 (Sections 18–26 commenced; Rules 17–21 commenced).
- **Physical/functional status as of this compilation:** Per multiple legal-press sources (LiveLaw, Mondaq, dpdpa.com tracker — secondary, not government-verified in this session), as of mid-2026 the Board **had not yet had its Chairperson or Members appointed and sworn in** — i.e., it exists in law but was reported to be **not yet operationally functioning** as a regulator. A MeitY communication dated **6 May 2026** (addressed to Union Ministry Secretaries, State/UT Chief Secretaries, and MeitY's subordinate offices) sought nominations for Search-cum-Selection Committee consideration for the Chairperson/Member posts, with a further related notification on **6 June 2026**. **This is a fast-moving fact and the chatbot should flag it as time-sensitive** — by the time an end user asks, appointments may have been made. The chatbot should avoid asserting a specific current Board composition without a live check.
- Until the Board is fully staffed, no complaint can practically be adjudicated even though the statutory complaint-filing mechanism is nominally live — a materially important caveat for any user asking "can I complain to the Board today."

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.2 Consent Manager framework — practical timeline
body:
- Legal registration mechanism (Section 6(9), Rule 4, First Schedule) does not commence until **~13/14 November 2026** (one year after Rules notification).
- Because the Board itself was reportedly not fully staffed as of mid-2026 (see 4.1), there is a live tension flagged by industry commentary (ComplianceHub.Wiki, cited as secondary/unverified) that the **Consent Manager registration deadline may arrive before there is a functioning Board to actually process registrations** — the chatbot should present this as an open practical risk rather than a resolved fact, and should not assert a specific registered Consent Manager exists without a live check of the Board's website (which the Rules themselves designate as the authoritative public list, per Rule 4(2)(a)).

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.3 Phased implementation timeline (consolidated, cross-referencing Parts 1 and 2)
body:
| Phase | Date | What goes live |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 13/14 November 2025 (Gazette publication date) | Act: Board establishment/composition/procedure (ss.18–26), definitions (s.2), misc. provisions (ss.35, 38–43), TRAI/RTI consequential amendments (s.44(1),(3)). Rules: Board appointment/procedure/staffing (Rules 1, 2, 17–21). |
| 2 | ~13/14 November 2026 (1 year after) | Act: mandatory Consent Manager registration (s.6(9)), Board's power over Consent Manager registration breaches (s.27(1)(d)). Rules: Consent Manager registration and obligations (Rule 4). |
| 3 | ~13/14 May 2027 (18 months after) | Act: the substantive core — grounds for processing, notice, consent mechanics, legitimate uses, all Data Fiduciary/SDF obligations, all Data Principal rights and duties, cross-border transfer restriction, exemptions, most Board enforcement powers, IT Act amendments including omission of s.43A (ss.3–17, 27 except (d), 28–34, 36, 37, 44(2)). Rules: notice content, security safeguards, breach intimation, retention/erasure, children's/disability consent, SDF obligations, Data Principal rights mechanics, cross-border transfer, research exemption, Tribunal appeal, information-calling (Rules 3, 5–16, 22, 23). |

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.4 Government's "don't wait" compliance messaging
body: Multiple legal-press sources (S.S. Rana & Co., Mondaq, referencing MeitY public statements) report that MeitY has **publicly urged organisations not to wait until the final commencement date** to begin DPDP compliance, given the scale of process/technology changes needed (consent flows, breach-response playbooks, DPO appointments for likely-SDFs, children's-data age-verification tooling). A compliance-focused chatbot should convey that **legal enforceability begins in phases as above, but prudent practice is to build toward full compliance well before the May 2027 deadline** — this is a business-risk framing point, not a legal-effective-date point, and the two should not be conflated in chatbot answers.

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.5 The RTI Act amendment (Section 44(3)) — a live controversy worth flagging
body: As detailed in Part 1 (Section 44), the DPDP Act replaces RTI Act s.8(1)(j)'s previous *balancing test* (a public-interest override could compel disclosure of personal information) with a **blanket exemption for "information which relates to personal information."** Civil-society and transparency advocates (e.g., Internet Freedom Foundation, in commentary flagged during this research though not independently re-verified beyond the search-snippet level) have argued this could be used to **withhold information about public officials' assets, discretionary decisions, or misconduct** that was previously disclosable under the old public-interest test. The official PIB explainer's counter-framing (see Part 1, s.44) is that RTI s.8(2)'s public-interest override remains available at the *authority's* discretion, and that the amendment merely "codifies" the Puttaswamy privacy-as-fundamental-right position. **A compliance chatbot fielding RTI-related questions should present both the letter of the amendment and this genuine, unresolved interpretive debate, not just the government's framing.**

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.6 Interaction with the (former) IT Act Section 43A regime
body: Until Section 44(2) commences (~May 2027), the **existing IT Act, 2000 Section 43A regime** (compensation for negligent failure to protect "sensitive personal data" under the SPDI Rules, 2011) **remains in force in parallel** with the DPDP Act's institutional/Board provisions that are already live. Only at the May 2027 mark does s.43A get omitted and effectively superseded by the DPDP Act's penalty regime. A chatbot should not tell a user that s.43A/SPDI Rules, 2011 are "already repealed" — they are not, as of the compilation date.

part: PART 4 — OTHER AUTHORITATIVE CLARIFICATIONS A COMPLIANCE CHATBOT SHOULD KNOW
heading: 4.7 No amendments identified to the DPDP Act itself
body: As of the compilation date, no Parliamentary amendment to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 itself has been identified — the only post-enactment legal instruments found are (a) the commencement notification(s) under s.1(2), and (b) the DPDP Rules, 2025 made under s.40. The Central Government's power under **Section 42** to amend the penalty Schedule (capped at doubling) has also not, per this research, been exercised.

part: KEY UNCERTAINTIES (please verify independently before relying on these in a legal-accuracy-critical answer)
heading: Key uncertainties to verify independently
body:
1. **One-day date discrepancy for the Rules' notification/effective date.** The Rules PDF's own gazette dateline reads "New Delhi, the 13th November, 2025" for G.S.R. 846(E), and the gazette issue itself is headed "No. 760] NEW DELHI, THURSDAY, NOVEMBER 13, 2025." However, the official PIB explainer document states the Rules were "notified on **14 November 2025**." This may reflect a difference between the notification's signing/dating and its actual public release/effective date, or simply an imprecision in the PIB summary. **Recommend treating "13–14 November 2025" as the safe way to state this date until the exact Gazette e-publication timestamp is confirmed against egazette.gov.in.**

2. **Commencement notification G.S.R. 843(E) (bringing the Act itself into force) was not independently retrieved and parsed as a standalone gazette PDF in this research** — its existence, number, date, and the exact section-by-section commencement list in Part 1/4.3 above were triangulated from consistent secondary legal-press reporting (Bar & Bench, S.S. Rana & Co., dpdpa.com's timeline page) that all converge on the same list, but this research was not able to locate and directly parse the G.S.R. 843(E) gazette PDF itself the way it did for the Act and the Rules. **This is the single most important item to verify against egazette.gov.in or indiacode.nic.in before treating the section-by-section commencement list as unimpeachable**, even though multiple independent secondary sources agree on it.

3. **No official MeitY FAQ document on the DPDP Act was located** (see Part 3 in full). It is possible one exists behind meity.gov.in's 403-blocked pages that this research's automated tools could not access. A manual browser check of `meity.gov.in/content/digital-personal-data-protection-act-2023` is recommended before telling end users no such FAQ exists at all.

4. **Data Protection Board appointment status is a moving target.** This knowledge base states the Board was reportedly unstaffed (no Chairperson/Members sworn in) as of mid-2026 per secondary press sources. This is exactly the kind of fact that can go stale within weeks; the chatbot should ideally be re-verified against current news or the Board's own website (once operational) rather than treated as a permanently fixed fact.

5. **No government-issued list of countries/territories restricted under Section 16 (cross-border transfer) has been identified.** Rule 15 leaves this to future "general or special order" by the Central Government; this research found no evidence such an order has yet been issued. If a user asks "which countries can I transfer data to/from," the accurate answer as of the compilation date is that **no restriction list has been notified yet** — but this should be re-checked, since it is exactly the kind of gap the Government may fill at any time.

6. **Whether any post-notification corrigendum or minor amendment to the DPDP Rules, 2025 has since been issued** (beyond the original 13 Nov 2025 notification) was not exhaustively ruled out — only that no such amendment surfaced in this research's searches. Given the Rules' schedules contain granular numeric thresholds (net worth, user-count thresholds, retention periods), any future corrigendum could change a number cited verbatim in Part 2 above.

7. **Draft-to-final Rules comparison in Part 2 (Rule 13(4)/(5) additions) relies on secondary legal-commentary characterisation** (Bar & Bench / S.S. Rana & Co. / Legal500) of what changed between the January 2025 draft and the November 2025 final text; this research verified the **final Rule 13(4)/(5) text itself** directly (it is accurately reproduced above), but did not independently re-parse the January 2025 draft PDF side-by-side to confirm the claimed delta. Treat the *final* Rule 13 text as high-confidence (directly sourced); treat the *characterisation of what changed from the draft* as secondary/medium-confidence.

8. **This knowledge base paraphrases rather than reproduces the Act/Rules verbatim** in the interest of chunkable, LLM-context-friendly summaries. For any answer where the exact statutory wording is legally dispositive (e.g., a client dispute over precise phrasing of a definition or an obligation), the chatbot should be configured to pull and quote the verbatim text from the official PDFs (URLs in the Master Source List) rather than rely solely on this summary.
